newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 7.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- RESERVES BLOW TO LABOUR PLANS

The government has revealed that they have already spent part of the contingency reserve set aside for the financial year, which began yesterday. This will make it difficult for an incoming Labour chancellor to meet existing targets for public spending. Treasury figures show a 200 million stg cut in the reserve and the money is understood to have been diverted to meet the costs of the BSE cattle crisis.
-- EX-HERITAGE CHIEF FACES MPS' CENSURE

Chris Green, head of business consulting at Alexander Gibb & Partners, the civil engineering firm, could face censure by the House of Commons public accounts committee over financial irregularities while he was chief executive of English Heritage. Green is also a director of Eurotunnel and consultant to Connex, the train operator. A Conservative member of the committee, Michael Stern, has asked for the names of Green's new employers so that copies of the findings can be sent to them.
-- BRITAIN AND SPAIN ALONE IN OPTIMISM

According to a survey for the venture-capital group 3i, managers of small businesses in Britain and Spain are the only optimists left in Europe still confident about their countries' economy and their own commercial prospects. The survey suggests these managers expect to recruit more staff in the near future. It says businesses in the two countries are planning investments in computers, plant, training and research and most of them expect profits and turnover to improve during the year.
THE TIMES
-- ASTRA TO OFFER EMERGENCY SATELLITE FOR DIGITAL TV

The company that owns the Astra satellites, SES, has told BSkyB that its plans for digital television need not be affected by the delay in launching the Astra 2A satellite. The satellite, which was to trasnmit the new channels, was built by the Hughes Corporation of the US. The start of digital will now depend on the formation of a joint company designed to finance the set-top boxes that viewers will need to get access to the channels.
-- LABOUR READY TO CARRY OUT REVENUE SALE

The Labour Party has announced it will go ahead with a government scheme to sell off the Inland Revenue's 450 offices in a 2.5 billion stg privatisation. The accountant Deloitte and Touche is close to completing an evaluation of the project, to be completed in July. Several bidders have already expressed interest in the sale, including Nomura. This could bring 500 million stg into the Exchequer and be worth as much as two billion stg over the next 20 years.
-- CITY EXPECTS RISE IN RATES

Roger Young, director-general of the Institute of Management, says the City is bracing itself for a sharp rise in interest rates after the general election. He predicts rates will need to rise as high as eight percent to head off inflationary pressures. He claims economic confidence is turning into over-confidence and that there are signs inflation is about to "raise its ugly head".
THE GUARDIAN
-- COST OF RECESSION IS 6,000 STG PER HEAD

Figures from independent analyst Datamonitor show the wealth-shrinking effect of the recession has wiped 6,000 stg off the average person's net worth during the past seven years. From a peak in 1989, wealth per head has fallen, in real terms, from 31,851 stg to 25,442 stg last year. Britons are shown as thriftier than in the past and are concerned with an "earnest" attempt to accumulate assets.
-- DEMOGRAPHIC TIME BOMB A 'DAMP SQUIB'

Britain Divided, the first study of poverty in all its forms during the 18 years of Conservative Party rule, is set to challenge claims by both the Tory and Labour Party that there can be no more public spending unless voters accept a high tax burden. Authors of the document claim demands on the welfare state will grow as the number of unemployed people dependent on those in jobs increases, the so-called demographic time bomb.
-- SAUNDERS IN NEW BATTLE

Ernest Saunders, former chief of Guinness, is in a legal dispute with David Elias, the entrepreneur and former Wells Fargo banker. Elias is threatening to sue Saunders for allegedly having destroyed up to one billion stg of value in the Harpur-Gelco information systems company, which Elias built up from the early 1980s. Saunders has instructed solicitors to sue Elias for libel over the allegations.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- TOBACCO GIANT GOES ON TRIAL

The tobacco industry on both sides of the Atlantic faces a troubling time as a lawsuit bought by the estate of Jean Connor, a dead smoker, is to start in a Florida courtroom against America's second biggest cigarette manufacturer RJ Reynolds. The lawsuit says RJ Reynolds is responsible for the habit that killed Connor and that it knowingly withheld information from her about the risks of smoking.
-- ENGINEERS' PAY SETTLEMENTS RESTRAINED

According to the Engineering Employers' Federation, engineering pay is bucking the trend towards higher earnings. Pay settlements in January were up 3.05 percent on last year. Head of employment affairs at EEF, David Yeandle, said employers are maintaining a sensible attitude towards settlements in a time of economic uncertainty. Industry observers were sceptical about the results, with one saying engineers have seen extra money even though the level of settlements does not seem high.
-- MORE GAS PRICE CUTS IN PIPELINE

Selective price cuts by British Gas, after an unexpectedly large number of households deserted the company in the South-west of England, has lead to independent gas suppliers stepping up their fight for domestic competition in the Southeast. Independent suppliers believe British Gas is planning a sudden introduction of selective price reductions, known as "Value Plus", in Kent and Sussex if Ofgas approves the new tariff package on offer in the Southwest.
